chapters.example: Walk the checklist on a real setup: (1) Helmet — shade set for the job, lens uncracked, safety glasses on underneath. (2) Skin — flame-resistant jacket buttoned, gauntlets over the sleeves, no synthetic shirt, pockets empty of lighters. (3) Machine and cables — no damaged insulation, work lead clamped to clean metal close to the joint. (4) Area — combustibles cleared or covered, extinguisher in reach. (5) Fumes — extraction arm positioned so the plume rises into the hood, not past your face. Each item names the injury it prevents: shade prevents arc eye, the jacket prevents UV burns, extraction prevents fume fever.
chapters.heading: The pre-arc checklist: PPE, machine, area, fumes
chapters.review: Name the four parts of your pre-arc checklist and one injury each part prevents — without looking back.
chapters.text: Welding concentrates intense light, heat, electricity, and fume in one small work area, so its safety rules are specific and enforceable. Welding, cutting, and brazing are covered by OSHA 29 CFR 1910 Subpart Q, and PPE by 1910.132 (general), 1910.133 (eye and face), and 1910.134 (respiratory protection). The arc emits ultraviolet and infrared radiation that can burn eyes and skin in seconds; looking at an arc unprotected causes arc eye, a painful corneal burn that may not be felt until hours later. Wear a helmet with the correct filter shade for the process and amperage — arc welding commonly calls for shades 10 to 14, darker as amperage rises, from the ANSI/AWS Z49.1 shade guide — safety glasses with side shields underneath and whenever the helmet is up, a flame-resistant jacket, leather gauntlet gloves, and covered skin with no cuffs or open pockets to catch sparks. Never carry matches or lighters in a pocket while welding. For fumes, keep your head out of the plume: position work and body so fume rises away from your breathing zone, and use local exhaust ventilation. Galvanized steel produces zinc oxide fume that can cause metal fume fever; stainless can generate hexavalent chromium. When the shop procedure, the manufacturer's instructions, and the standard differ, follow the most protective instruction and ask before you improvise.

chapters.example: Your bay has a parts washer 12 feet away, cardboard at 20 feet, and a wall opening at 30 feet. Applying the rule: the parts washer cannot move, so it gets a fire-resistant cover; the cardboard can move, so it leaves the radius; the wall opening is covered so sparks cannot pass through. The permit records the location, the time window, each precaution verified, the fire watch's name, and the post-work watch end time — and the handover note says what was welded, where sparks could have traveled, what was checked, and when the watch ends.
chapters.heading: The 35-foot rule, the permit, and the fire watch
chapters.review: A combustible sits 20 feet from your weld and cannot be moved. What exactly do you do before striking an arc?
chapters.text: Most welding fires are not caused by the arc itself but by hot particles reaching fuel the welder never saw — sparks and slag travel surprising distances, lodge in cracks and wall openings, and smolder out of sight before they flame. OSHA 1910.252(a) therefore sets a distance rule: do not weld or cut where combustibles are within 35 feet unless they cannot be moved — then protect them with fire-resistant covers, cover floor and wall openings within range so sparks cannot pass through, and sweep floors clean of combustibles. Shops control the rest of the risk with a hot-work permit system on the NFPA 51B model: a permit authorizing individual inspects the area, confirms the precautions on the permit are actually in place, and authorizes hot work for a defined place and time. The fire watch is a named person with an extinguisher who watches during the work and for the watch period after it ends, because smoldering fires start late. The permit is not a formality: work outside its place, time, or precautions is unauthorized work.

chapters.example: Four jobs, four calls: (a) Outdoor structural repair in wind — SMAW or FCAW-S, because their shielding survives wind that would strip a gas shield. (b) Thin stainless tubing in a food plant — GTAW, for precise heat control and a clean, sanitary finish. (c) Heavy plate production indoors — FCAW-G or GMAW, for high deposition rates with no wind problem. (d) Ornamental thin-gauge shop work — GTAW or GMAW on low settings, where control and appearance matter more than speed.
chapters.heading: Four processes, one job: choosing how the weld gets made
chapters.review: Why does wind rule out GMAW outdoors but not SMAW? Answer in one sentence naming the shielding difference.
chapters.text: Every arc process does the same fundamental job — an electric arc melts the edges of the work and a filler metal while shielding protects the molten puddle from the oxygen and nitrogen in air that would make the weld porous and weak. The four processes differ in how filler is delivered and how shielding is produced, and those differences decide where each earns its place. SMAW (stick) uses a flux-coated electrode: the flux decomposes into shielding gas and a slag blanket. It is simple, portable, tolerant of wind and imperfect surfaces, and works in all positions — which is why it dominates field, structural, and repair work — at the cost of speed and cleanup. GMAW (MIG) feeds wire continuously through the gun with gas shielding: fast and clean indoors, but wind strips its shielding. FCAW carries flux in a tubular wire — self-shielded (FCAW-S) for outdoor work or gas-shielded (FCAW-G) for heavy indoor deposition. GTAW (TIG) uses a non-consumable tungsten and separate filler: the most precise and cleanest process, and the slowest, chosen for thin material, stainless, and work where appearance and control rule. Choosing a process weighs material, thickness, position, environment, quality requirements, and production rate.

chapters.example: Setup record for a GMAW job on 1/4-inch mild steel: machine — CV output (wire processes self-adjust on CV); polarity — DCEP, verified at the terminals against the wire's specification; wire — the diameter the manufacturer's chart lists for 1/4-inch steel; voltage and wire feed speed — the chart's starting pair for that wire and thickness, noted with the chart page; gas — the chart's shielding gas at 25 cfh, mid-range of the 20–30 band. Then a test bead on scrap confirms the chart's starting point before the real joint is touched.
chapters.heading: Power sources, polarity, and the settings that decide the bead
chapters.review: A machine is rated 60% duty cycle at 200 A. How many minutes of arc time at 200 A does it allow in a 10-minute period?
chapters.text: Welding power sources hold one of two outputs steady. A constant-current (CC) machine holds amperage nearly fixed while voltage varies with arc length; it serves SMAW and GTAW, where the welder controls the arc by hand. A constant-voltage (CV) machine holds voltage steady and lets current follow the wire feed; it serves GMAW and FCAW, where the machine self-adjusts the arc. Connecting a process to the wrong output type is a setup error you catch before striking an arc. Polarity decides where the heat goes. In DC electrode positive (DCEP, 'reverse polarity') the electrode is positive — the standard choice for most SMAW electrodes and for GMAW, giving stable arcs and deep penetration. In DC electrode negative (DCEN, 'straight polarity') more heat concentrates at the workpiece, suiting GTAW on steels because it keeps the tungsten cooler. AC splits the difference and adds oxide cleaning on the positive half-cycle, the usual choice for GTAW on aluminum. A swapped lead is invisible until the arc misbehaves — read polarity at the terminals and confirm it against the specification. In GMAW, voltage sets arc length and bead profile while wire feed speed sets amperage and deposition; start from the manufacturer's chart for your wire and gas. Shielding gas flow is typically 20 to 30 cubic feet per hour — too little starves the shield, too much creates turbulence that pulls air in. Duty cycle rates how long a machine can weld at a given output in ten minutes: 60 percent at 200 amps means six minutes of arc time, then rest for the machine.

chapters.example: A long seam bows after welding. The plan for the identical second part: tack both ends and the middle first so the seam cannot walk; clamp the part flat to a strongback; weld in short segments, alternating sides and skipping around the part so heat input balances instead of accumulating at one end; use the lowest amperage that still fuses the joint; let each segment cool before its neighbor is welded. Each choice answers the same physics — shrinking weld metal pulls, so you restrain the part and spread the pull evenly.
chapters.heading: Metals, carbon, and why parts bow: metallurgy for welders
chapters.review: Why does a medium-carbon steel joint get a preheat plan when a mild-steel joint of the same thickness does not?
chapters.text: Welders sort metals first by whether they are built on iron. Ferrous metals — carbon steels, alloy steels, stainless steels, cast iron — are iron-based and make up most welded work. Non-ferrous metals contain no significant iron: aluminum, copper alloys, titanium, magnesium — each with its own oxide behavior, heat conduction, and filler requirements. When a metal cannot be identified with confidence, the job stops for verification rather than guessing: the wrong filler or procedure can ruin a joint. Within steels, carbon content drives weldability. Low-carbon (mild) steel, up to roughly 0.30 percent carbon, is the most weldable common metal and usually needs no preheat at moderate thickness. As carbon rises, the heat-affected zone (HAZ) — the band beside the weld that got hot without melting — can harden and crack, so medium- and high-carbon steels call for preheat, controlled interpass temperature, and sometimes post-weld treatment; you verify the plan and measure with a temperature-indicating tool. Distortion is the other heat effect: weld metal shrinks as it cools and pulls the part toward the weld. You control it before it happens — balanced tacking, clamping, welding sequence that distributes heat, and no more heat input than the joint needs.

chapters.example: Decode from memory, then check: 1G — plate flat, groove weld, welding on top with gravity helping the puddle. 2G — plate vertical, groove axis horizontal. 3G — plate vertical, weld travels vertically. 4G — plate overhead. 2F — fillet on a tee with the joint horizontal. 3F — fillet welded vertically. In the shop, a frame's corner joints take fillets; a pressure plate seam takes a groove weld with a prepared bevel — the joint decides the weld, and the position code prices the difficulty.
chapters.heading: Five joints, two weld families, and the position codes
chapters.review: A drawing calls for 3F. Describe the joint, the weld type, and the direction of travel in one sentence.
chapters.text: Every welded connection is built from five joint geometries, defined by how the members meet. In a butt joint the members lie in the same plane, edge to edge — the standard for plate and pipe seams. A tee joint meets at roughly ninety degrees, one member standing on another's face. A lap joint overlaps one member over the other, common in sheet work and repairs. A corner joint meets two edges at an angle, forming boxes and frames, and an edge joint joins parallel edges, used mainly on thin material. Two weld families cover nearly all structural work. A groove weld is deposited in a prepared opening — a square edge on thin material, or a V, bevel, U, or J preparation cut into thicker edges so the arc can reach the root and fuse the full thickness. A fillet weld fills the corner where two surfaces meet, in tee, lap, and corner joints. Positions are coded so any welder can read the difficulty at a glance: for plate groove welds, 1G flat, 2G horizontal, 3G vertical, 4G overhead; for fillets, 1F through 4F in the same order. Flat is the easiest position and the one to learn first; overhead is the most demanding because gravity works against the puddle.

chapters.example: Decode: a right-triangle fillet glyph below the reference line, '1/4' to its left, '3' to its right. Reading in order: the glyph below the line puts the weld on the arrow side; the triangle means a fillet weld; 1/4 is the leg size in inches; 3 is the length in inches. The instruction is: a 1/4-inch fillet weld, 3 inches long, on the arrow side of the joint. Now write the reverse: a single-V groove symbol above the line with a circle at the arrow joint means a V-groove weld on the other side, welded all around the joint.
chapters.heading: Reading the welding symbol: the contract on the reference line
chapters.review: A symbol sits above the reference line. Which side of the joint gets the weld, and how do you know?
chapters.text: A fabrication drawing cannot carry a paragraph of instructions for every weld, so the industry compresses weld requirements into a standardized symbol system — in North America, AWS A2.4. The symbol is a contract: weld type, size, length, location, and special instructions in a few strokes, and the welder is responsible for producing exactly what it says. Every symbol is built on a horizontal reference line. An arrow line connects the reference line to the joint, pointing at the exact location to be welded; a tail at the opposite end carries specifications or process notes when needed. The weld symbol sits on the reference line, and its placement carries meaning: a symbol below the reference line specifies the weld on the arrow side (the side the arrow points at); above the line, the other side; on both sides, both. Size is written to the left of the symbol, length to the right; intermittent welds add pitch — the center-to-center spacing. A circle at the joint of arrow and reference line means weld all around; a flag means a field weld, made at erection rather than in the shop. Misreading any of this produces the wrong weld with perfect technique — which is why this workbook makes you decode cold and write symbols for a classmate to decode.

chapters.example: Diagnose a failed bead from its evidence. The bead is narrow, high-crowned, and ropey with undercut grooves at both toes: the puddle never spread, which reads as travel too fast and current too low for the joint — the metal arrived faster than it could wet in. The correction changes one variable at a time: raise amperage into the electrode's range, then slow travel until the puddle width steadies and the toes wet in. The next bead is logged beside the failed one — date, process, settings, position, and what changed — because the log is what turns one fix into permanent skill.
chapters.heading: Striking the arc and running the bead: the three controls
chapters.review: Your bead is narrow and ropey with undercut toes. Name the two most likely causes and the first variable you would change.
chapters.text: Every bead begins with a clean start, and sloppy starts leave defects that persist through the finished weld. In SMAW, start with a scratch motion — draw the electrode lightly across the surface like striking a match — or a tap straight down and up; the instant the arc strikes, lift to a working arc length and move into the joint. In GMAW, trim the wire to a short, consistent stickout and pull the trigger so gas coverage is established as the arc initiates. Restarts get the same care: strike slightly ahead of the existing crater, move back to remelt it fully, then continue — a restart that piles metal on a cold crater traps slag and lacks fusion where the joint is already weakest. Once running, you control the bead with three variables. Arc length — for SMAW, roughly the diameter of the electrode's core wire — governs voltage and focus: too long wanders, spatters, and undercuts; too short sticks and crowns the bead. Angles work in two planes: the work angle positions the electrode relative to the joint, and the travel angle tilts it in the direction of travel — stick is a drag technique at roughly 10 to 20 degrees from perpendicular. Travel speed ties it together: too fast leaves a narrow, ropey bead with undercut edges; too slow piles a wide, overheated bead that can overlap the toes and trap slag. Watch the puddle: consistent width, edges wetting into both sides, even ripples behind you. A stringer bead runs straight — the default for root passes and thin material; a weave oscillates to widen fill and cap passes.

chapters.example: Read three cut faces. Face one: drag lines fine and nearly vertical, top edge sharp — speed and pressures were right; log it as the standard. Face two: drag lines sweep back at a hard angle and the bottom edge holds slag — the torch outran the oxidation, so slow travel or check that the tip size matches the thickness. Face three: top edge melted and rounded, kerf wide at the top — too much preheat or too slow; reduce preheat flame or pick up speed. Each face is a diagnosis, not a grade: state what the lines say, then the adjustment.
chapters.heading: Cutting processes: burning steel on purpose, and reading the cut face
chapters.review: Why can oxy-fuel cut carbon steel cleanly but not stainless — and what process do you choose for stainless instead?
chapters.text: Oxy-fuel cutting does not melt steel away; it burns it. A torch preheats a spot on carbon steel to its kindling temperature — a bright cherry red — then a lever releases a jet of pure oxygen that reacts with the hot iron; the resulting iron oxide is blown out of the cut, leaving a kerf. Because the process is a chemical reaction with iron, it works beautifully on carbon steel and poorly on metals whose oxides resist it: stainless steel and aluminum form refractory oxide skins and are not cut cleanly by oxy-fuel. Plasma cutting works differently — an electric arc and compressed gas blast through any conductive metal — which is why plasma is the choice for stainless and aluminum. The welder's oxy-fuel control variables are tip size matched to thickness, correct fuel and oxygen pressures for that tip, a neutral preheat flame, steady travel speed, and tip distance. The cut face reports your technique in its drag lines: fine, near-vertical lines mean correct speed; lines that curve back sharply mean you outran the cut; a melted, ragged top edge means too slow or too much preheat. Oxy-fuel safety is its own discipline: acetylene is unstable under pressure and must never be used above 15 psi regulator pressure; cylinders are stored and used upright and secured, valves opened only as far as the manufacturer directs, and every connection leak-tested before lighting.

chapters.example: Inspect a coupon finding by finding. (1) Scattered surface pores, middle third: porosity — a discontinuity; measured against the criteria for this joint, the cluster exceeds the allowed amount, so it is a defect: disposition repair, cause hunt points at a damp electrode or lost shielding. (2) A groove at the toe measured beyond the criteria depth: undercut — defect, repair by blending or a corrective pass. (3) Even ripples, edges wet in, reinforcement inside profile limits: discontinuities at most — accept and record. The record names each finding's type, location, and measured size before any disposition is written, because the disposition is only as good as the measurement behind it.
chapters.heading: Visual inspection: discontinuity versus defect, judged against criteria
chapters.review: A pore and a crack are both discontinuities. Why does only one of them always fail the weld?
chapters.text: Inspection begins with a distinction that governs everything else: a discontinuity is any interruption in the ideal weld — a pore, a slag pocket, a profile irregularity — while a defect is a discontinuity that exceeds the acceptance criteria of the governing code and therefore requires repair or rejection. Every weld contains discontinuities at some scale; the inspector finds them, measures them, and judges them against the criteria that apply to that joint, such as the visual acceptance criteria in AWS D1.1. That is why visual testing (VT) is a discipline and not a glance: adequate lighting, direct access to the surface, simple measuring tools, and a written criteria reference in hand. Know the surface findings. Porosity: round holes where gas was trapped as the metal solidified — causes are contamination, moisture, excessive arc length, or lost shielding. Slag inclusion: non-metallic material trapped in the weld, typically between passes where interpass cleaning was rushed. Undercut: a groove melted into the base metal at the toe and left unfilled — it thins the member and concentrates stress, from excessive current, speed, or poor angle. Overlap: weld metal rolled over the toe without fusing, hiding a lack-of-fusion line beneath. Incomplete fusion and incomplete penetration mean the weld never bonded or never reached the root — among the most serious findings because the joint's cross-section is silently smaller than designed. Cracks are the most serious of all, and hydrogen-induced cold cracks can appear in hardenable steels up to two days after welding — one reason final inspection of susceptible work is not always immediate.

chapters.example: Prove a 36 in × 48 in frame square before tacking. The diagonal of a true rectangle is the hypotenuse: √(36² + 48²) = √(1296 + 2304) = √3600 = 60 inches — the 3-4-5 triangle scaled by twelve. Measure both diagonals: 60 and 60 means square, tack it. If you read 60 and 61-1/4, the frame is racked by 1-1/4 inches — pull the long diagonal's corners in until both read 60, then tack. This is the same measurement the Weld Booth Lab asks you to compute, done here with a tape instead of a keyboard.
chapters.heading: Fabrication workflow: print to part, verified at every step
chapters.review: Both diagonals of your frame read equal, but the frame is 1/8 inch short on one side. Is it acceptable? What decides?
chapters.text: Fabrication is welding embedded in a sequence, and most failed parts fail before the arc is struck. The sequence runs: read the print and its symbols; build the cut list — every part, its material, thickness, and finished dimensions; verify material identity and condition; lay out and cut the parts; prepare the joint edges; fit the assembly up and check it; tack it; weld it in a planned sequence; then measure, inspect, finish, and document. Each step verifies the one before it, because an error discovered after welding costs ten times what it cost at layout. The welder's measuring kit is simple and unforgiving: a steel tape read to the sixteenth, a combination square, a framing square, a scribe or soapstone, and levels. Layout discipline means measuring from a common datum rather than chaining measurements part to part, so errors do not stack; marking cut lines and bend lines distinctly; and checking diagonals to prove squareness — equal diagonals on a rectangular frame mean it is square, and a difference is the amount of rack to pull out before tacking. Tolerances come from the print: a dimension without an explicit tolerance still carries the sheet's general tolerance, and 'close enough' is a decision the print makes, not the welder. Fit-up sets the root opening, alignment, and bevel condition the weld must bridge: too tight starves penetration, too wide invites burn-through, and edges are cleaned to bright metal at the joint because mill scale, rust, paint, and oil become porosity and inclusions if they are welded over.

chapters.example: Sort the three documents on a real job. The WPS says: GMAW, this wire, this gas, these settings, flat and horizontal positions — the recipe every welder on the job follows. The PQR is the lab record behind the WPS: the test coupon welded to that recipe, bent and passed — the proof the recipe works. Your performance qualification record says: you personally welded test coupons under a qualified WPS, in these positions, and your bends passed — the proof you can execute the recipe. A qualification plan names the process and positions you will test, the facility you will test with, and the practice coupons you must pass consistently in the shop first.
chapters.heading: Certification: performance qualification, not a course grade
chapters.review: An employer asks for your WPS. What is wrong with that request, and which document actually proves your qualification?
chapters.text: Welder certification is performance qualification: documented proof, produced by welding actual test coupons under controlled conditions, that a welder can deposit sound metal with a given process, in given positions, on given materials and thicknesses. It is not a written-exam credential and it is not awarded for completing a course — this course prepares you for it and teaches you its system; the qualification itself is earned at the test. In the United States the dominant system is the American Welding Society's. Under AWS D1.1, the Structural Welding Code — Steel, a welder welds test plates or pipe following a Welding Procedure Specification (WPS) — the recipe: process, filler, parameters, positions. The WPS itself is qualified by a Procedure Qualification Record (PQR), the documented test that proved the recipe produces sound welds. The welder's own result is the performance qualification record: visual inspection plus destructive mechanical tests, principally guided bend tests that fold the weld and its heat-affected zone to expose internal unsoundness. The AWS Certified Welder program standardizes that test across a national network of Accredited Test Facilities, so a credential earned at one facility is recognized at others. Qualification is also perishable in a specific way: continuity. A welder who does not weld with a qualified process for more than six months loses continuity in it and must requalify — so certified welders log their work.

chapters.example: A capstone self-inspection entry reads: 'Fillet coupon — legs measured 1/4 in and 9/32 in against a 1/4 in specification: the 9/32 leg is oversized, recorded as a discontinuity within profile tolerance, disposition accept with note. Stop crater, groove coupon — crack 3/16 in long running from the crater: defect under any criteria, disposition reject my own coupon; cause — crater not filled at the stop, travel ended abruptly; correction — fill the crater with a pause and slight back-step before breaking the arc, then re-run the coupon.' That entry — measurement, disposition, cause, correction — is the standard your record is graded against.
chapters.heading: The capstone: produce the coupon, then inspect your own work first
chapters.review: Your self-inspection finds nothing wrong with either coupon. Why should that make your instructor look harder, not easier?
chapters.text: The capstone is the course's practical assessment, performed in the shop under instructor supervision and graded on evidence, not attendance. Working from a supplied print and a specified procedure, you produce two coupons: a tee-joint fillet weld of the specified leg size, and a groove-welded plate coupon in the position your instructor assigns from your lab progression. For each coupon you own the full chain the course taught: read the print and state the requirement aloud; set up the machine and verify polarity and settings; prepare and fit the joint to the specified root opening and alignment; tack; weld in a planned sequence; clean; and present the finished coupon with its completed weld log. Nothing is graded that is not documented — an undocumented coupon is an unfinished coupon. Before your instructor inspects anything, you inspect your own work with the visual method: measure the fillet legs with a fillet gauge and record actual sizes; list every discontinuity with its location and measured size; write a disposition for each against the criteria, with cause and correction for anything you reject in your own work. Your written self-evaluation is part of the grade — the trade needs welders whose self-inspection an instructor can trust, and the comparison between your findings and your instructor's is where the remaining gaps get named and a practice plan gets agreed.

chapters.example: Build your ten-question self-quiz from the lessons you found hardest, the way the assessment will ask them — as decisions. Weak on symbols? Write: 'A fillet symbol sits above the reference line with 5/16 at its left — what do you weld, where, and how big?' Weak on defects? Write: 'A bead shows a groove at the toe and a ropey profile — name the defect, its two likely causes, and your first correction.' Answer the quiz cold a day later, record what you missed, and re-study exactly those lessons before the assessment — the miss list is the study plan.
chapters.heading: Final review: the portfolio is the proof
chapters.review: In your two-minute employer summary, which four things must you name? Say them in order.
chapters.text: The final assessment samples the whole course the way the trade will test you: not topic by topic in isolation, but as connected judgment. Safety comes first and is weighted accordingly — the OSHA Subpart Q framework, PPE selection by process and amperage, fume hazards and their controls, the 35-foot rule, fire watch duties, and the cylinder rules. Process knowledge follows: how SMAW, GMAW, FCAW, and GTAW differ in filler delivery and shielding, and how those differences choose the process for a job. The technical core — polarity and power sources, metallurgy and the heat-affected zone, joints and positions, and the AWS A2.4 symbol system — is assessed as working knowledge: interpret a symbol, diagnose a defect from its description, reason from a defect back to its cause at setup or technique. Read each question for the decision it is really asking about. Most wrong answers are not random; they are the plausible shortcut — the weld made without the permit check, the setting chosen without the chart, the discontinuity waved through without a measurement. Your portfolio is the other half of the evidence: weld logs, setup records, inspection practice, the fabrication packet, the capstone package, and this workbook, assembled in order, with any gap named and a plan to close it. Together they are what you hand an employer: processes you can run, positions you have practiced, inspection skills you hold, and the qualification test you are scheduled for.
